reasoning.Student A:
I prefer w > x > y > z. Under the usual student-proposing deferred-acceptance (DA) mechanism, truthfully reporting my preferences is a dominant strategy, so I should submit my true ranking.

Consider priorities and others' preferences: many applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y will be highly contested. However, I have top priority (rank 1) at both w and y, and rank 2 at x and z. Because I already have highest priority at my most-preferred school w, there is no strategic advantage to misrepresenting preferences to chase a school that is more popular. Ranking any less-preferred school above a more-preferred one could only risk getting a worse match. Therefore I will submit my sincere ranking.

With my top priority at x (rank 1) and many other applicants favoring y first, I have a strong chance at x but a weaker chance at y (my priority at y is 2). Under standard student-proposing deferred acceptance (the usual matching rule in these problems), it is strategy-proof for students to report their true preferences. Misrepresenting preferences (e.g., ranking y above x) could only risk losing a school I prefer and have higher priority for. Therefore I should submit my sincere ranking x > w > y > z.
